Malaybalay is a relatively new city. It was declared a city through Republic Act 08490 in 1998 and celebrated its fourteenth year of being a city on March 22, 2012. Malaybalay is the capital city of Bukidnon Province, located right at the center of Mindanao Island of the Philippines. Aside from being the provincial capital of Bukidnon, with the provincial offices  and  the  hospital  of  the  province,  it  is  also  the  educational  center,  where

To the east of the city is the Pantaron mountain range, which separates Bukidnon from the province of Agusan Sur. To the west is the Mount Kitanglad Range National Park (MKRNP), to the north is the municipality of Impasug-ong, and to the south is the city of Valencia. At the heart  of Malaybalay is the  Sawaga River,  whose tributary rivers and creeks originate in the Mt. Kitanglad Range Natural Park. On the eastern side of the city
is the bigger Pulangui River, whose tributaries come from the Pantaron mountain range.

The city has about 65% of its 108,259 hectares of land classified as forestland, and only about  35%  as  alienable  and  disposable,  which  means  it  can  be  titled  and  privately owned. The city is composed of 46 barangays – the smallest administrative division of the  country  –  and  of  these,  13  are  considered  part  of  the  urban  center,  five  are urbanizing, and 28 are rural. Based on the 2010 census, the city has a total population of 153,085 with an annual growth rate of 2.16% (based on 2000-2010), which is higher
than the national growth rate of 1.90% (NSO, 2012).

About 36% of the city’s population lives in the urban center, which covers only 5% of the land area; 15% of the population lives in the urbanizing barangays, which is about 10% of the land area; and 85% of the population lives in the rural barangays, which is about  49%  of  the  city’s  land  area  (CPDO  Malaybalay,  2014).  The  city  is  now  clearly expanding  to  the  urbanizing  barangays,  which  now  have  a  2.6%  annual  population growth  rate,  while  the  urban  and  rural  barangays  have  only  3%  and  1.5%  growth,

Compared  to  the  other  islands  in  the  Philippines,  Mindanao  -  where  Malaybalay  is located- is relatively safe from weather related hazards. Fewer tropical cyclones make landfall in Mindanao than in other parts of the country. In the last 15 years, only six typhoons  crossed  Mindanao  Island,  compared  to  the  yearly  typhoons  that  visit  the
islands of Luzon and some part of Visayas.

According to the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (cited in Narisma et al., 2012), typhoons hit Mindanao Island only about every 10 years. Typhoon Sendong, which made landfall in Mindanao Island in December 2011 was a 10-year typhoon. It hit two of the most populated and vulnerable areas, Cagayan de Oro City and Iligan City. It also affected the smaller  towns  of  Libona,  Baungon,  and  several  villages  of  Valencia  City  in  Bukidnon, which are located along the river. The typhoon brought a lot of rain, resulting in flash flooding in the mentioned areas, which killed around 1,257 people and injured around 6,071 more people (NDRRMC, 2011). About the same time a year later, for the first time Malaybalay  City  experienced  the  signal  3  Typhoon  Pablo  that  brought  strong  winds. Fortunately, there were no casualties and not many damages to properties. It brought strong winds which scared 2,887 non-farming households, and it has also affected 3,178
farmers with around 4,183 hectares of farmlands(City Agriculture Annual Report 2012).

Given  the  City’s  experiences  with  typhoons,  the  CDRRMC  is  in  consensus  identifying typhoons as a medium threat to the different sectors of the city – social, infrastructure, economic, and environment.
